summary:
Región de Atacama stands under Chile's national legal framework, and a visitor's expectations there are set by national law rather than by regional ordinance. Legal gender recognition rests on Gender Identity Law 21,120, in force since 27 December 2019: adults may change their registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry without therapy or surgery, while applicants aged 14 to 18 must apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents. On 9 April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the 'over 14 years old' wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, a ruling that applies only to that case.

The 2012 Zamudio Law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, was extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and birth certificates have offered a third sex option for intersex children since 2006.

Outright International's Chile country dossier, published 12 March 2026, records no Atacama-specific legal, incident or enforcement finding and no division-level information, so the region is assessed at the national score. The dossier's Chile findings match the national framework: self-determination legal gender recognition since 2019, marriage and adoption since March 2022, hate-crime coverage of sexual orientation and gender identity since 2012, and the third sex option since 2006.

Movilh's XXIV annual report (HECHOS 2025, published March 2026) places Atacama at 1.83% of nationally documented abuse cases, a year-on-year rise of 7.69%. Nationally the report counts a record 3,620 cases and complaints of discrimination in 2025, up 27.1% and the highest in 24 years. Only Valparaíso (-17.56%) and Metropolitana (-14.35%) fell, while the other 14 regions rose, and Movilh reads the shift as hatred expanding into regions with less public debate. Atacama's share is therefore a small but rising fraction of a national total that is itself rising steeply.

Two Atacama-specific positives appear in the same report. The Municipality of Atacama convened the commune's first Pride march, and Atacama and Puerto Varas became the first regions to hold Pride marches during 2025, expanding the movement's territorial visibility.

Transphobic violence remains documented nationally. A young trans man was murdered in 2023 in a killing covered up for 24 hours and described in national reporting as Chile's largest hate crime, the perpetrator an acquaintance who confessed. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour at a Santiago hotel, where the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Entry and removal rules reference gender identity. The Migration and Immigration Law of 11 April 2021 bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that recognised asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity.

Detention carries specific rules. Gendarmería de Chile's national director signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees, providing placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives overseeing implementation, including access rules for trans visitors.

Restrictive proposals are active but non-binding. On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report, 56 votes to 30 with 6 abstentions, a non-binding recommendation to eliminate the Gender Identity Support Program, restrict minors' progressive autonomy, ban hormonal treatment for minors and repeal the circular protecting gender identity in schools.
tangentialFactors:
The regional picture sits inside a national trend that Movilh describes as geographic broadening. Of Chile's 16 regions, 14 recorded more discrimination cases in 2025 than in 2024, and only Valparaíso and Metropolitana recorded declines. Movilh's reading is that hostility is spreading into regions where public debate about sexual and gender diversity is thinner, which would place Atacama among the areas where visibility gains and case growth are occurring together rather than in sequence.

Visibility and reported harm rise in the same period in Atacama. The region's first Pride march convened by the Municipality of Atacama and its place, with Puerto Varas, among the first regions to hold Pride marches during 2025 coincide with a 7.69% year-on-year increase in its share of nationally documented abuse cases. Whether increased reporting reflects increased incidence, increased willingness to report, or both is not resolved by the sources.

Legislative and executive turbulence around trans minors' care continues at national level. The 2025 Budget Law's section 46 barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents until the Constitutional Court annulled it on 9 January 2025 by seven votes to three, and in November 2025 Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program through the 2026 Budget Law. The Chamber of Deputies' 15 May 2025 approval of the CEI 57 report adds a non-binding recommendation layer that does not change the law in force.

Chile's protections compare favourably with neighbouring jurisdictions on paper: self-determination gender recognition, marriage equality since March 2022, and statutory asylum protection referencing gender identity are all in force, while documented lethal violence shows that formal protection and street-level risk coexist.
localsOnly:
Residents' access to care is shaped by several instruments. The public health system has funded sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013, and a 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centres to register transgender patients by their social name. Circular 7 of June 2024 suggested deferring the initiation of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published, and the Medical College noted that physicians may still prescribe.

The Ministry of Health-run support programme continues after Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program through the 2026 Budget Law in November 2025, with support still provided in medical centres. The Crece con Orgullo programme has operated since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17. Outright International records the congressional exclusion of the Gender Identity Support Program from the 2026 budget bill as part of a 2025-26 rollback, an action condemned by civil society groups and the national ombuds for children.

Minors seeking legal gender recognition apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents, since the Gender Identity Law applies directly to adults and only through the courts to those aged 14 to 18; people under 14 cannot use the law, although the statute recognises them as transgender. The Constitutional Court's 9 April 2025 decision on the 'over 14 years old' wording applies only to the case before it.

Intersex children are recorded with a third sex option on birth certificates. In detention, Gendarmería's protocol provides placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations, with a standing committee overseeing implementation.
outOfScopeNotes:
Outright International's Chile dossier carries no Atacama-specific legal, incident or enforcement finding and no division-level information, so no regional enforcement pattern can be confirmed from it; the regional assessment rests on national findings plus Movilh's regional table.

Movilh's 2024 regional share for Atacama is not reproduced in the 2025 edition, so the 1.83% figure and its 7.69% year-on-year rise cannot be checked against a stated prior-year baseline from this source. Movilh's counts are documented cases and complaints of discrimination, not prosecutions or convictions, and the sources do not say how many involved trans victims specifically.

The Constitutional Court's 9 April 2025 ruling on the age wording is stated to apply only to the case in which it was brought, and its effect on other under-14 applications is not sourced here. The CEI 57 report approved on 15 May 2025 is non-binding, and the sources do not record whether any of its recommendations have since been introduced as legislation.

No Atacama-specific incident data, police complaint figures or regional judicial outcomes are present in the inventory, and general crime conditions in the region are outside this assessment.
